title: Ecology: understand it, use it, remember it
scope: The 33 teacher StudyMate terms, recovered Environments and Populations packet, teacher Matter and Energy in Food Webs notes, ecology key and symbiosis slides. Exact publisher-only readings and the wider Science course are not certified complete.

chapters.title: From one organism to the biosphere
teach: Use nesting and contrast to make the words meaningful: one organism, a same-species population, interacting populations as a community, and organisms plus abiotic conditions as an ecosystem. The biosphere is the global life scope. A biome groups broad climate-and-community regions; it is not simply one step in the local nested list.

For every example, say what is included and what is left out. A community includes living populations; an ecosystem also considers nonliving conditions. Biotic and abiotic are describing words, not two new organization levels.

model.prompt: Original park model: one oak → all oaks of that species in the park → interacting living populations → those populations with water, light and soil conditions. Explain what changes at each step.
model.reasoning: Identify exactly which organisms, environment or relationship is being described. Choose a term whose meaning fits those details. Compare the closest alternative and explain why it does not fit. Keep the conclusion limited to the given evidence and conditions.
model.answer: The single oak is an organism; all local oaks of that species are a population; the interacting living populations form a community; adding water, light and soil conditions gives an ecosystem. The biome is a broad climate/community region, and the biosphere is Earth’s global life scope. Biotic/abiotic describe factors rather than add nesting levels.

terms.meaning: One individual living thing.
terms.example: A scientist records the behavior of one individual snail.
terms.nonexample: All deer in a forest form a population, not one organism.
terms.boundary: Single-celled life also counts; animal or plant examples are not the whole category.

terms.meaning: Individuals of the same species living in a particular area.
terms.example: All eastern gray squirrels living in one park are counted.
terms.nonexample: Deer, trees and fungi together are not one population.
terms.boundary: Area and species boundaries matter; all living things together are not one population.

terms.meaning: The populations of different species living and interacting in an area.
terms.example: Researchers study the interacting fish, algae, insects and bacteria in a pond, leaving nonliving conditions outside this list.
terms.nonexample: Including water temperature and sunlight makes the model an ecosystem rather than only a community.
terms.boundary: Do not confuse one same-species population with a multi-species community.

terms.meaning: A community of organisms interacting with its nonliving environment.
terms.example: A pond model includes organisms, water, light, temperature and their interactions.
terms.nonexample: Only the fish population omits other organisms and nonliving conditions.
terms.boundary: The boundary is chosen for a question; organisms and materials can cross it.

terms.meaning: The parts of Earth where life exists; the global scope of life and ecosystems.
terms.example: A model includes every region of Earth where life exists.
terms.nonexample: One pond is not the entire biosphere.
terms.boundary: Biosphere is a level/region of life, whereas biotic describes living factors.

terms.meaning: A large ecological region characterized by climate and typical communities.
terms.cue: Climate + characteristic communities over a large region.
terms.example: A large region is characterized by a cold climate and typical plant and animal communities.
terms.nonexample: One individual tree is not a biome.
terms.boundary: A biome can contain many local ecosystems; boundaries are broad models.

terms.meaning: Describing nonliving physical or chemical environmental factors.
terms.example: A pond study measures water temperature and dissolved oxygen.
terms.nonexample: A living tree is not an abiotic factor.
terms.boundary: Use temperature, sunlight, water and minerals as clear cases; distinguish biological origin when discussing dead material.

terms.meaning: Describing the living components and biological influences in an environment.
terms.cue: Bio: living things and their influence.
terms.example: A study focuses on trees, fungi and insects rather than temperature.
terms.nonexample: Sunlight is not a biotic factor.
terms.boundary: Use living organisms and their biological effects as clear examples. Temperature and sunlight are abiotic.

options: A scientist records the behavior of one individual snail.
All eastern gray squirrels living in one park are counted.
Researchers study the interacting fish, algae, insects and bacteria in a pond, leaving nonliving conditions outside this list.
A pond model includes organisms, water, light, temperature and their interactions.
guided.rationale: One individual living thing. Single-celled life also counts; animal or plant examples are not the whole category.

chapters.title: Resource use, limits and introductions
teach: A species can share a habitat yet use different resources. Explain a niche with what, when and how resources are used. Then identify the condition that currently limits a population and how that affects supportable population size.

Native and invasive describe different things: natural regional occurrence versus a harmful nonnative introduction. Not all introduced organisms are invasive. An adaptation is an inherited trait related to conditions, not a decision an individual makes because it needs to change.

model.prompt: Original garden model: a plant introduced by people spreads and shades out native seedlings. The lost light limits seedling growth. Identify origin, harm, resource mechanism and the evidence needed to estimate longer-term population support.
model.reasoning: Identify exactly which organisms, environment or relationship is being described. Choose a term whose meaning fits those details. Compare the closest alternative and explain why it does not fit. Keep the conclusion limited to the given evidence and conditions.
model.answer: The plant is nonnative, and its documented harmful spread supports invasive status. Reduced light is a limiting factor for seedlings. Its niche includes its resource use and interactions; estimating carrying capacity needs more resource and population evidence. No individual acquires an inherited adaptation simply because it needs one.

terms.meaning: A species occurring naturally in a region, rather than introduced there by people.
terms.example: Historical evidence shows a plant occurred naturally in this region before people introduced new plants.
terms.nonexample: A species introduced by people last year is not native merely because it survives.
terms.boundary: A native species need not thrive everywhere; use the specific region.

terms.meaning: A nonnative species that causes, or is likely to cause, harm in the introduced environment.
terms.cue: Introduced + harmful risk; not just new.
terms.example: People introduce a plant that spreads rapidly and reduces native habitat.
terms.nonexample: A nonnative garden plant with no established harm is not automatically invasive.
terms.boundary: Nonnative alone is insufficient; investigate harm and context.

terms.meaning: A resource or condition that restricts population growth or size.
terms.example: A population has ample food but too few safe nesting sites to increase.
terms.nonexample: An abundant resource is not necessarily the factor currently restricting growth.
terms.boundary: A limiting factor can be a condition, not only a scarce food resource.

terms.meaning: The largest population size an environment can sustain under its current conditions.
terms.example: A habitat can sustain at most about 60 deer under current food and water conditions.
terms.nonexample: The number of animals present today is not automatically the capacity.
terms.boundary: It is population-specific and can change when resources/conditions change.

terms.meaning: A species’ role, resource use and interactions within its environment.
terms.example: A study explains when a bird feeds, which insects it eats and where it nests.
terms.nonexample: The street address or place alone describes habitat, not the whole niche.
terms.boundary: A niche includes interactions with living and nonliving conditions; sharing a habitat does not mean identical niches.

terms.meaning: An inherited trait that can improve survival or reproduction in a particular environment.
terms.cue: Trait fitted to conditions over generations.
terms.example: An inherited camouflage pattern makes some prey harder to see in their habitat.
terms.nonexample: One animal deciding to change color is not an inherited adaptation.
terms.boundary: Adaptations can help with food, water, protection or reproduction. An individual does not inherit a new trait just because it needs one.

options: Historical evidence shows a plant occurred naturally in this region before people introduced new plants.
People introduce a plant that spreads rapidly and reduces native habitat.
A population has ample food but too few safe nesting sites to increase.
A habitat can sustain at most about 60 deer under current food and water conditions.
guided.rationale: A species occurring naturally in a region, rather than introduced there by people. A native species need not thrive everywhere; use the specific region.

chapters.title: Feeding roles and diets
teach: Separate broad role, diet and pathway level. A consumer can be a herbivore, carnivore or omnivore. Predator/prey identifies the participants in a particular feeding interaction. Tertiary consumer identifies a position on one stated path.

Start from a producer and follow arrows. Primary eats a producer; secondary eats primary; tertiary eats secondary. A tertiary consumer need not be the highest organism in a longer path. An omnivore can occupy more than one level, so always name the path.

model.prompt: Trace this pathway: duckweed → snail → fish → heron.
model.reasoning: Start with the producer. Count one consumer level at each feeding arrow. The snail eats the plant; the fish eats the snail; the heron eats the fish.
model.answer: Duckweed is the producer, the snail primary, the fish secondary and the heron tertiary on this pathway. The fish is predator of the snail and prey of the heron.

terms.meaning: Organisms that build food from inorganic materials using an energy source.
terms.cue: Make food; do not create energy.
terms.example: Algae use light to build food that can support a pond web.
terms.nonexample: A rabbit eating plants is a consumer, not a producer.
terms.boundary: Classroom examples use sunlight/photosynthesis; some producers use chemical energy. They convert energy rather than create it.

terms.meaning: An organism obtaining food by eating organisms or their material.
terms.example: A rabbit obtains food by eating grass.
terms.nonexample: A photosynthetic plant is not a consumer merely because it uses energy.
terms.boundary: Consumer levels depend on the particular feeding path.

terms.meaning: A consumer that eats only plants or other producers in the diet described.
terms.example: In a stated diet, a rabbit feeds on plants.
terms.nonexample: A predator eating only animals is not a herbivore.
terms.boundary: Use the stated food. Algae are producers too; herbivores can eat producers without being harmless to them.

terms.meaning: A consumer that eats only animals in the diet described.
terms.example: An owl in the stated example feeds on mice.
terms.nonexample: A consumer feeding on both berries and insects is an omnivore.
terms.boundary: Use the actual described diet; predator and carnivore overlap but are not identical terms.

terms.meaning: A consumer that feeds on producer material and animals.
terms.example: A raccoon eats fruit and insects.
terms.nonexample: Eating two different plants alone does not establish omnivory.
terms.boundary: Consumer level can change with the feeding path; classify by actual food source.

terms.meaning: A tertiary consumer eats a secondary consumer in the specified feeding pathway.
terms.example: Path: grass→grasshopper→frog→snake.
terms.nonexample: An animal eating a producer is not tertiary on that path.
terms.boundary: Count from a producer along the stated path. A tertiary consumer need not be the last animal in every possible chain.

terms.meaning: An organism that captures and consumes prey.
terms.example: An owl captures and eats a mouse.
terms.nonexample: An animal harmed by a hunter is the prey in that interaction.
terms.boundary: Predator/prey describes a relationship; one organism can be predator in one interaction and prey in another.

terms.meaning: An organism captured and consumed by a predator.
terms.example: An owl captures a mouse for food.
terms.nonexample: The animal doing the hunting is the predator in that interaction.
terms.boundary: A prey organism can also be a predator of something else; roles depend on the relationship.

options: Algae use light to build food that can support a pond web.
A rabbit obtains food by eating grass.
In a stated diet, a rabbit feeds on plants.
An owl in the stated example feeds on mice.
guided.rationale: Organisms that build food from inorganic materials using an energy source. Classroom examples use sunlight/photosynthesis; some producers use chemical energy. They convert energy rather than create it.

chapters.title: Models and processing remains
teach: A chain traces one energy route; a web combines routes; an energy pyramid compares available energy by level. These models answer different questions and omit details. Do not read a pyramid as a map or assume it shows the exact number of individuals.

A scavenger consumes dead remains. Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down remains and waste. Both help process material, but they are not identical mechanisms. Matter is returned and reused; usable energy transfers and disperses rather than cycling back identically.

model.prompt: Original pond model: algae feeds snails and insect larvae, both eaten by fish. Trace one chain, then the whole web. Compare usable energy by level, and add decomposers acting on material from every level.
model.reasoning: Identify exactly which organisms, environment or relationship is being described. Choose a term whose meaning fits those details. Compare the closest alternative and explain why it does not fit. Keep the conclusion limited to the given evidence and conditions.
model.answer: Algae→snail→fish is one food chain; adding algae→insect larva→fish makes connected paths in a food web. An energy pyramid represents less usable energy reaching higher levels. Decomposers break down remains/wastes from all levels; scavengers consume dead remains. Nutrients can return to the environment while energy transfers and disperses.

terms.meaning: One linear feeding pathway showing energy transfer among organisms.
terms.example: A model traces one path: grass→rabbit→fox.
terms.nonexample: Multiple branching feeding pathways form a web, not just one chain.
terms.boundary: The chain is a simplified pathway; decomposers act on material from all levels.

terms.meaning: A model showing multiple connected feeding relationships.
terms.example: A diagram connects several producers and consumers through multiple feeding paths.
terms.nonexample: One unbranched feeding sequence alone is a food chain.
terms.boundary: Arrows show food-energy transfer; a model omits some real relationships.

terms.meaning: A model showing decreasing usable energy available at higher feeding levels.
terms.example: A triangular model compares usable energy at producer and consumer levels, showing less upward.
terms.nonexample: A map of where organisms live is not an energy pyramid.
terms.boundary: Energy is transferred and dispersed, not destroyed; the model is not the same as a pyramid of numbers.

terms.meaning: Organisms such as many fungi and bacteria that break down remains and wastes.
terms.example: Fungi break down fallen leaves and release nutrients into the environment.
terms.nonexample: A vulture swallowing a dead animal is primarily a scavenger, not the same process as fungal decomposition.
terms.boundary: Decomposers act on material from all feeding levels; matter cycles but usable energy is not recycled back identically.

terms.meaning: An organism that consumes dead organisms or their remains.
terms.example: A vulture eats the remains of a dead animal.
terms.nonexample: A fungus chemically breaking down a log is a decomposer example, not the same feeding process as a vulture.
terms.boundary: Scavengers and decomposers both help process remains but do so differently.

options: A model traces one path: grass→rabbit→fox.
A diagram connects several producers and consumers through multiple feeding paths.
A triangular model compares usable energy at producer and consumer levels, showing less upward.
Fungi break down fallen leaves and release nutrients into the environment.
guided.rationale: One linear feeding pathway showing energy transfer among organisms. The chain is a simplified pathway; decomposers act on material from all levels.

chapters.title: Effects on both partners
teach: Symbiosis is the relationship noun; symbiotic is the describing adjective. These refer to close cross-species associations. They do not guarantee both partners benefit. Read the effects on each participant before choosing a more specific classification.

Use an effects table: mutualism is benefit/benefit, parasitism is benefit/harm, commensalism is benefit/no known effect. Host identifies the provider of habitat/resources; it does not by itself establish harm. Explain what evidence would change your conclusion.

model.prompt: Original association model: gut organisms receive food and shelter while supplying useful vitamins to an animal. Name the host, explain the benefit to each, and distinguish the relationship noun from its adjective.
model.reasoning: Identify exactly which organisms, environment or relationship is being described. Choose a term whose meaning fits those details. Compare the closest alternative and explain why it does not fit. Keep the conclusion limited to the given evidence and conditions.
model.answer: The animal is the host because it supplies habitat/resources. The described vitamin-producing partners and animal each benefit, so this case is mutualism. The relationship noun is symbiosis and the adjective is symbiotic. Harm to the host would instead support parasitism; benefit with no partner effect would support commensalism.

terms.meaning: Describing a close association between organisms of different species.
terms.example: A sentence describes a close, lasting association between two different species.
terms.nonexample: Two unrelated animals briefly passing each other are not enough evidence of a close association.
terms.boundary: The close relationship is not always mutually beneficial; look for the actual effects.

terms.meaning: A close association between organisms of different species.
terms.example: A question asks for the general noun covering close relationships between different species, including mutualism and parasitism.
terms.nonexample: Two same-species animals competing briefly is not the intended cross-species association.
terms.boundary: Both organisms do not have to benefit. Identify the effects on each participant.

terms.meaning: An organism providing habitat or resources for another organism.
terms.example: A deer supplies living habitat and food resources to a tick.
terms.nonexample: The organism receiving food from a harmed partner is the parasite, not that partner’s role as host.
terms.boundary: A host is not necessarily harmed; check the particular relationship.

terms.meaning: A relationship in which a parasite benefits while its host is harmed.
terms.cue: Plus for parasite; minus for host.
terms.example: A tick obtains food from a deer while harming the deer.
terms.nonexample: Both partners benefiting is mutualism.
terms.boundary: Harm matters; not every organism living on another is a parasite.

terms.meaning: One participant benefits while the other has no known benefit or harm.
terms.example: A small organism gains shelter from another, with no measured effect on its partner.
terms.nonexample: Benefit for one and harm to the other is parasitism.
terms.boundary: The classification depends on evidence about both participants in the described conditions.

terms.meaning: A relationship in which both species receive a benefit.
terms.example: An insect receives nectar while its visit pollinates the plant. Both benefit in this described case.
terms.nonexample: Living nearby does not prove mutual benefit.
terms.boundary: Name a benefit to each participant; context matters.

options: A sentence describes a close, lasting association between two different species.
A question asks for the general noun covering close relationships between different species, including mutualism and parasitism.
A deer supplies living habitat and food resources to a tick.
A tick obtains food from a deer while harming the deer.
guided.rationale: Describing a close association between organisms of different species. The close relationship is not always mutually beneficial; look for the actual effects.

chapters.title: Photosynthesis
teach: Sunlight supplies energy. Plants use water and carbon dioxide to build sugar, storing chemical energy, and release oxygen. Producers convert energy; they do not create it.

model.prompt: A sunflower receives light, water and carbon dioxide. Is the light a material ingredient of its sugar?
model.reasoning: Separate matter from energy. Water and carbon dioxide supply atoms; light supplies energy.
model.answer: The plant stores some light energy in the chemical bonds of sugar and releases oxygen. It converts energy rather than creating it.

options: Sunlight supplies energy. Plants use water and carbon dioxide to build sugar, storing chemical energy, and release oxygen. Producers convert energy; they do not create it.
All organisms use the same resources in the same amounts.
Every change in a population has exactly one possible cause.
Energy is created by consumers and destroyed by producers.
guided.rationale: Sunlight supplies energy. Plants use water and carbon dioxide to build sugar, storing chemical energy, and release oxygen. Producers convert energy; they do not create it.

chapters.title: Population density
teach: Population density is the number of individuals per unit of area or volume. Compare equal areas or divide the population by area. More crowded populations may compete more when resources are limited.

model.prompt: A one-hectare plot has 8 beetles; a two-hectare plot has 10. Which is denser?
model.reasoning: Divide each count by its area: 8 ÷ 1 = 8; 10 ÷ 2 = 5.
model.answer: The smaller plot is denser: 8 beetles per hectare compared with 5. A larger count does not always mean greater density.

guided.prompt: Which rule correctly explains population density?
options: Population density is the number of individuals per unit of area or volume. Compare equal areas or divide the population by area. More crowded populations may compete more when resources are limited.
All organisms use the same resources in the same amounts.
Every change in a population has exactly one possible cause.
Energy is created by consumers and destroyed by producers.
guided.rationale: Population density is the number of individuals per unit of area or volume. Compare equal areas or divide the population by area. More crowded populations may compete more when resources are limited.

chapters.title: Marine, freshwater and terrestrial ecosystems
teach: Marine ecosystems contain salt water, such as oceans and coral reefs. Freshwater ecosystems, such as lakes and streams, have very little dissolved salt. Terrestrial ecosystems are on land. Compare climate, water, soil and living populations when evaluating ecosystem health.

model.prompt: Compare a mountain stream, an ocean tide pool and a desert.
model.reasoning: Look at the environment: very low-salt water, salty seawater, or land.
model.answer: The stream is freshwater; the tide pool is marine; the desert is terrestrial. All three can contain producers and consumers.

guided.prompt: Which rule correctly explains marine, freshwater and terrestrial ecosystems?
options: Marine ecosystems contain salt water, such as oceans and coral reefs. Freshwater ecosystems, such as lakes and streams, have very little dissolved salt. Terrestrial ecosystems are on land. Compare climate, water, soil and living populations when evaluating ecosystem health.

Energy is created by consumers and destroyed by producers.

chapters.title: Resources, shelter and changing limits
teach: Water, light, temperature and soil conditions can affect survival. Different organisms need different amounts. Shelter can protect animals from weather and predators. A resource becomes limiting when its availability restricts growth. Irrigation supplies water to plants; it does not supply sunlight.

model.prompt: A seedling grows slowly in a dark cupboard despite wet soil. Would adding more water fix the stated problem?
model.reasoning: Identify what is scarce. The soil is already wet; light is missing.
model.answer: The evidence points to light as a limiting factor. Add suitable light while keeping other conditions comparable to test that explanation.

chapters.title: Competition and resource sharing
teach: Competition occurs when organisms need the same limited resource. Intraspecific means within one species; interspecific means between different species. A browser eats leaves and shoots of shrubs or trees; a grazer mainly eats grasses. Describe the actual foods used rather than assuming all plant eaters use identical resources.

model.prompt: Two species of birds both need a few available nesting holes.
model.reasoning: They are different species and share a limited resource. The resource is shelter, not necessarily food.
model.answer: This is interspecific competition. Birds of the same species competing for those holes would be intraspecific competition.

guided.prompt: Which rule correctly explains competition and resource sharing?
options: Competition occurs when organisms need the same limited resource. Intraspecific means within one species; interspecific means between different species. A browser eats leaves and shoots of shrubs or trees; a grazer mainly eats grasses. Describe the actual foods used rather than assuming all plant eaters use identical resources.

chapters.title: Follow the feeding pathway
teach: An arrow runs from food toward the organism receiving its energy. On grass → insect → frog → snake, the insect is primary, frog secondary and snake tertiary. If a snake eats a mouse that ate grass, the snake is secondary on that path. Count from the producer every time; an animal has no single permanent consumer level.

model.prompt: Trace clover → caterpillar → small bird → hawk.
model.reasoning: Start with clover, the producer, and count feeding steps. Each arrow points from food to eater.
model.answer: The caterpillar is primary, the bird secondary and the hawk tertiary on this particular path.

options: An arrow runs from food toward the organism receiving its energy. On grass → insect → frog → snake, the insect is primary, frog secondary and snake tertiary. If a snake eats a mouse that ate grass, the snake is secondary on that path. Count from the producer every time; an animal has no single permanent consumer level.

Energy is created by consumers and destroyed by producers.

chapters.title: Energy transfer and the energy pyramid
teach: In a simple energy-pyramid model, about 10% of energy at one feeding level transfers to the next. The remainder is used in life processes and spreads largely as heat. Energy is conserved; less remains available to the next feeding level. About 10% transferred is different from 10% lost.

model.prompt: A model gives producers 8,000 energy units. Estimate the amount at the next two levels using 10% transfer.
model.answer: About 800 reaches primary consumers and 80 reaches secondary consumers. The rest is not destroyed; it is used and dispersed, largely as heat.

guided.prompt: Which rule correctly explains energy transfer and the energy pyramid?
options: In a simple energy-pyramid model, about 10% of energy at one feeding level transfers to the next. The remainder is used in life processes and spreads largely as heat. Energy is conserved; less remains available to the next feeding level. About 10% transferred is different from 10% lost.
All organisms use the same resources in the same amounts.
Every change in a population has exactly one possible cause.
Energy is created by consumers and destroyed by producers.
guided.rationale: In a simple energy-pyramid model, about 10% of energy at one feeding level transfers to the next. The remainder is used in life processes and spreads largely as heat. Energy is conserved; less remains available to the next feeding level. About 10% transferred is different from 10% lost.

chapters.title: Matter cycles; energy flows
teach: Decomposers break down remains and wastes, returning matter to the environment. Plants can use some of those materials again. Scavengers consume remains; fungi and bacteria break them down further. Energy does not cycle back to plants in the same way nutrients do.

model.prompt: A fallen apple is broken down by fungi. Later a tree takes up some released nutrients. Has the apple energy returned unchanged to the tree?
model.reasoning: Trace the materials separately from energy. Some matter can be reused; energy is transferred and spreads as heat.
model.answer: The nutrient matter can cycle. The tree still needs a source of energy, usually sunlight, to build sugars.

guided.prompt: Which rule correctly explains matter cycles; energy flows?
options: Decomposers break down remains and wastes, returning matter to the environment. Plants can use some of those materials again. Scavengers consume remains; fungi and bacteria break them down further. Energy does not cycle back to plants in the same way nutrients do.
All organisms use the same resources in the same amounts.
Every change in a population has exactly one possible cause.
Energy is created by consumers and destroyed by producers.
guided.rationale: Decomposers break down remains and wastes, returning matter to the environment. Plants can use some of those materials again. Scavengers consume remains; fungi and bacteria break them down further. Energy does not cycle back to plants in the same way nutrients do.

chapters.title: Food-web changes and evidence
teach: A food web joins many feeding pathways. Removing one population can affect its predators, its food and competitors. Predict a likely change using the stated connections, and name other conditions that could change the result. A rise or fall in one population alone does not prove a single cause.

model.prompt: In a simple garden model, beetles eat leaves and birds eat beetles. Fewer birds visit.
model.reasoning: Follow the connections: less predation may allow more beetles, which may eat more leaves.
model.answer: More leaf damage is a reasonable prediction if other conditions stay similar. It is not a guarantee; weather and other predators could change the result.

questions.prompt: An insect gains shelter in a plant and protects it from leaf-eating animals. Which specific relationship fits the effects on the two species?
questions.rationale: A relationship in which both species receive a benefit. Name a benefit to each participant; context matters.

questions.prompt: A bird gains food by eating fruit and the plant gains seed dispersal. Which specific relationship fits the effects on the two species?
questions.rationale: A relationship in which both species receive a benefit. Name a benefit to each participant; context matters.

questions.prompt: A seedling gets water and carbon dioxide. Which missing input would directly power photosynthesis?
questions.rationale: Light powers the process that makes sugar.

questions.prompt: A leaf uses light to make sugar. Which gas supplies carbon atoms for that sugar?
questions.rationale: Carbon dioxide supplies carbon used to make sugar.

questions.prompt: A pond plant makes sugar in sunlight. Which gas can it release during this process?
options: Carbon dioxide as the main product
questions.rationale: Photosynthesis releases oxygen.

questions.prompt: How does a grass plant change the form of energy during photosynthesis?
options: Light energy becomes chemical energy stored in sugar.
Chemical energy in sugar becomes light energy.
Thermal energy becomes movement of the leaves.
The plant uses light to make energy from nothing.
questions.rationale: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in sugar.

questions.prompt: A student says soil is the direct source of the carbon in a plant’s sugar. Which correction fits the lesson?
options: Carbon dioxide supplies carbon, and light supplies energy.
Water supplies both the carbon and energy.
Oxygen supplies carbon, and soil supplies energy.
Light supplies the carbon, and sugar supplies the energy.
questions.rationale: The carbon comes from carbon dioxide, while the energy comes from light.

questions.prompt: A sample contains 32 beetles in 8 square meters. What is the population density?
questions.rationale: Divide the count by the area. 32 ÷ 8 = 4 per square meter.

questions.prompt: A sample contains 21 snails in 7 square meters. What is the population density?
questions.rationale: Divide the count by the area. 21 ÷ 7 = 3 per square meter.

questions.prompt: A sample contains 30 crickets in 5 square meters. What is the population density?
questions.rationale: Divide the count by the area. 30 ÷ 5 = 6 per square meter.

questions.prompt: A sample contains 24 seedlings in 12 square meters. What is the population density?
questions.rationale: Divide the count by the area. 24 ÷ 12 = 2 per square meter.

questions.prompt: A sample contains 45 worms in 9 square meters. What is the population density?
questions.rationale: Divide the count by the area. 45 ÷ 9 = 5 per square meter.

questions.prompt: A coral reef sits in warm, salty ocean water. Which category fits?
questions.rationale: Marine ecosystems occur in salt water.

questions.prompt: A low-salt river flows through a forest. Classify the ecosystem in the river itself.
questions.rationale: The river has very little dissolved salt, so its aquatic ecosystem is freshwater.

questions.prompt: A student studies the soil, insects and grasses of a prairie. Which category fits?
questions.rationale: A prairie is a land ecosystem.

questions.prompt: Which measurement most directly separates a freshwater lake from a marine bay?
questions.rationale: Freshwater and marine environments differ in dissolved salt.

questions.prompt: Which pair contains one freshwater and one marine ecosystem, in that order?
options: A low-salt pond and a coral reef
An ocean reef and a woodland
A prairie and a low-salt stream
A marine bay and an ocean reef
questions.rationale: The pond is freshwater and the coral reef is marine.

questions.prompt: Seedlings have enough water but receive almost no light. What change directly addresses the described limit?
options: Add more water without changing light.
Put more seedlings in the same tray.
Remove the soil without changing light.
questions.rationale: Light is the stated limiting resource.

questions.prompt: A hot pool lacks the cooler hiding spots needed by fish. What change best tests whether access to cooler shelter limits survival?
options: Provide a shaded refuge in otherwise comparable pools.
Add both food and more fish to the hottest pool.
Change the salt concentration and the number of fish together.
Compare pools while changing temperature, food and fish numbers together.
questions.rationale: A shaded refuge changes the proposed limit while other conditions stay comparable.

questions.prompt: A farm channel carries water from a reservoir to crop rows. What resource does it supply directly?
questions.rationale: Irrigation brings water to crops.

questions.prompt: Which change directly gives a small animal shelter from predators?
options: Add places it can hide under cover.
Add an open stretch of ground.
questions.rationale: Cover provides a place to hide.

questions.prompt: A classroom experiment keeps water and light equal while changing soil nutrients. What resource is the test comparing?
questions.rationale: Only the soil nutrient supply changes.

questions.prompt: Two robins of the same species need the same limited nesting site. Which term fits?
questions.rationale: Competition within one species is intraspecific.

questions.prompt: A rabbit and a grasshopper both eat the same scarce seedlings. Which term fits?
questions.rationale: They are different species using a shared limited resource.

questions.prompt: Two bird species use different foods and nest in different places. Which observation would support competition between them?
options: Both start needing the same scarce nesting holes.
One finds plenty of a food that the other never eats.
One uses a habitat the other never enters.
Both have enough space and continue using different resources.
questions.rationale: Competition requires overlap in a limited resource.

questions.prompt: A group of deer feeds mainly on leaves and twigs of shrubs. Which label describes that feeding behavior?
questions.rationale: Browsers feed mainly on woody plants, such as shrubs.

questions.prompt: Two species share the same water source during a drought. What would most directly reduce competition for that resource?
options: Make more water available to both species.
Add more individuals that need the same water.
Reduce the amount of water available.
Keep water scarce and add more users.
questions.rationale: Increasing the limited resource directly reduces pressure on it.

questions.prompt: In the chain grass → rabbit → fox, which is the primary consumer?
questions.rationale: The rabbit eats the producer and is the primary consumer.

questions.prompt: In algae → snail → fish → heron, which is the secondary consumer?
questions.rationale: The fish eats the snail, which is the primary consumer.

questions.prompt: In seeds → mouse → snake → hawk, which organism receives energy directly from the snake in this path?
questions.rationale: The arrow from snake to hawk shows the energy transfer.

questions.prompt: A raccoon eats berries on one path and a plant-eating insect on another. What changes?
options: The raccoon acts as a primary consumer on the berry path and secondary on the insect path.
The raccoon is a producer on the berry path and primary on the insect path.
The raccoon acts as secondary on the berry path and primary on the insect path.
The raccoon is tertiary on both paths.
questions.rationale: Consumer level depends on what the raccoon eats on each pathway.

questions.prompt: In leaves → beetle → lizard → snake, which organism eats the secondary consumer?
questions.rationale: The lizard eats the beetle and is secondary. The snake eats the lizard.

questions.prompt: The clover producer level has 4,000 units of available energy. Under the 10% model, about how much transfers to primary consumers?
questions.rationale: About 10% transfers in this model. 4,000 × 0.10 = 400 units.

questions.prompt: The algae producer level has 7,000 units of available energy. Under the 10% model, about how much transfers to primary consumers?
questions.rationale: About 10% transfers in this model. 7,000 × 0.10 = 700 units.

questions.prompt: The grass producer level has 2,200 units of available energy. Under the 10% model, about how much transfers to primary consumers?
questions.rationale: About 10% transfers in this model. 2,200 × 0.10 = 220 units.

questions.prompt: The seagrass producer level has 3,600 units of available energy. Under the 10% model, about how much transfers to primary consumers?
questions.rationale: About 10% transfers in this model. 3,600 × 0.10 = 360 units.

questions.prompt: The pond plants producer level has 4,500 units of available energy. Under the 10% model, about how much transfers to primary consumers?
questions.rationale: About 10% transfers in this model. 4,500 × 0.10 = 450 units.

questions.prompt: Fungi decompose fallen leaves. What can happen to some of the leaf matter?
options: It returns to the surroundings and can become part of another organism.
It is destroyed when the leaf disappears.
It can never enter another living thing.
questions.rationale: Decomposition returns materials to the environment for reuse.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares nutrients and usable energy in an ecosystem?
options: Nutrients can cycle, while usable energy flows through the system.
Usable energy cycles back to producers in exactly the same way as nutrients.
Nutrients and usable energy both remain forever in the same organism.
Nutrients disappear when organisms break down, while energy becomes new matter.
questions.rationale: Matter cycles. Energy is transferred and dispersed, so fresh energy inputs are needed.

questions.prompt: Which process makes material from a dead log available in the soil?
options: Fungi and bacteria break the log down.
The log makes sugar using sunlight.
A predator captures a living animal.
Wind moves the intact log without breaking it down.
questions.rationale: Decomposers break remains down and make some materials available again.

questions.prompt: A plant’s roots take up mineral nutrients that were released by decomposers. What does that show?
options: Materials from remains can reenter living organisms.
All energy in the remains has returned to the roots.
The decomposers made matter from nothing.
The minerals became sunlight before entering the plant.
questions.rationale: Nutrients from remains can move back into living organisms.

questions.prompt: A compost pile warms as microbes break down remains. Which interpretation fits?
options: Some energy disperses as heat while materials are made available for reuse.
The warmth proves that the microbes created new energy.
The warmth means all the original matter disappeared.
Heat sends all the original usable food energy back to plants.
questions.rationale: Decomposition moves materials and transfers energy, some of which disperses as heat.

questions.prompt: In a simplified chain algae → snails → fish, snails suddenly decrease. What is the best immediate prediction if other factors stay similar?
options: Less food for fish and less grazing on algae
More food for fish and more grazing on algae
Less food for fish and more grazing on algae
More food for fish and less grazing on algae
questions.rationale: Fewer snails mean fewer consumers of algae and less snail food for fish.

questions.prompt: In grass → rabbits → foxes, foxes decrease. What is a reasonable short-term prediction if other factors stay similar?
options: Rabbits face less predation and may increase.
Rabbits face more predation and may decrease.
Rabbits immediately lose their grass food source.
questions.rationale: Fewer foxes can reduce predation on rabbits.

questions.prompt: A bird eats both caterpillars and beetles. Caterpillars decrease. Which detail matters most for predicting what happens to the bird?
options: Whether enough beetles remain as another food source
Whether the caterpillars have the same color as beetles
Whether the birds and beetles have similar body sizes
Whether the plant leaves are green or yellow in a photo
questions.rationale: Alternate feeding paths can soften the effect of losing one food source.

questions.prompt: In plants → insects → frogs, the plant food supply falls. What is a reasonable prediction with other conditions similar?
options: Insects may decline, leaving fewer insects for frogs.
Insects gain food, so frogs immediately lose food.
Frogs gain energy directly from the missing plants.
The insects become producers to replace the plants.
questions.rationale: A smaller producer supply can affect consumers at several levels.

questions.prompt: A pond fish population falls after an insect decline. Why should scientists also measure oxygen and temperature?
options: Changes in fish numbers can have more than one cause.
The time sequence alone proves insects were the only cause.
Oxygen and temperature cannot affect fish survival.
A feeding connection makes other evidence irrelevant.
questions.rationale: A food-web link suggests a possible cause. Other conditions can also affect the population.
